# Random catalytic reaction networks

`random-catalytic-networks` · *Stadler, Fontana & Miller, 1993*

## Introduction

A random catalytic reaction network is the simplest chemistry in which
molecules make *other* molecules. There are `n` kinds of molecule, `X1` to
`Xn`, and they have no structure at all: no sequence, no shape, just a name.
What they can do is written in a table. For each pair of kinds, the table says
which kinds the pair helps to make, and how fast. When `X1` meets `X2`, for
instance, the pair may produce a new `X3`, and both `X1` and `X2` survive the
encounter, so they act as catalysts. Fill the table at random, put the
molecules in a stirred tank from which the surplus is constantly washed out,
and watch which kinds of molecule are still there at the end.

Peter Stadler, Walter Fontana and John Miller introduced the model in 1993.
They wanted a mathematical model of populations whose members are not
replicators, but interact to produce further objects "not necessarily of the
same type" (their paper's words). Chemistry is the obvious example: two
molecules react, and what comes out is fixed by the chemistry of what went in.
A whole set of objects can then copy itself, as a set, without any single
member copying itself, which they note may have happened in an early phase of
prebiotic evolution, before individual replicators existed. Their equation is
a generalisation of the replicator equation, and it
contains the replicator and Lotka-Volterra equations as special cases.

Chemart generates the model as a mathematical object: a network of
explicit reactions with random rate constants, meant to be integrated as
ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe it in
the chapter on evolution (book §7.2.9), as a model that goes one step beyond
the quasispecies, replicator and Lotka-Volterra equations (those three
entries are archived in Chemart).
Because the molecules have no structure, this entry is the *null model* for the
constructive chemistries that do. [AlChemy](alchemy.md),
[matrix chemistry](matrix-chemistry.md) and the
[automata reaction](automata-reaction.md) all have reactions of the same form,
`s1 + s2 -> s1 + s2 + s3`, but they compute the product `s3` from the
structure of `s1` and `s2` instead of reading it from a random table. Stadler
and colleagues point out that Fontana's Turing gas, the model behind AlChemy,
follows their equation, run as a stochastic process. Its nearest neighbours among the random
networks are the [Jain-Krishna model](jain-krishna.md), in which one molecule
catalyses the production of another, and
[Kauffman's autocatalytic sets](kauffman-autocatalytic-sets.md) and
[Bagley and Farmer's metabolism](bagley-farmer.md), in which the molecules
are polymers that join and split.

## How it works

### Molecules, reactions and the tank

Every reaction has the form

```
Xi + Xj -> Xi + Xj + Xk
```

with a rate constant `α` (alpha). The two reactants are catalysts: they are
not used up, and the new molecule `Xk` is made from raw material that is
assumed always available and is not tracked. When `k` is `i` or `j` the pair
copies one of its members, which the book calls *direct replication*. By
default Chemart leaves such reactions out, as in the book's main case, so no
kind of molecule can make more of itself directly.

Only relative concentrations matter. The tank is a *continuously stirred tank
reactor*: new molecules are made all the time, and a *dilution flux* `φ`
(phi) washes molecules out, all kinds at the same rate, so that the
concentrations always add up to 1. Each concentration therefore changes as

```
x_k' = (production of Xk) − x_k · φ
```

where the production of `Xk` is the sum, over all reactions that make it, of
the rate constant times the concentrations of the two reactants (mass action),
and `φ` is the total production of all kinds. A kind shrinks while its
production is less than its washout `x_k · φ`; a kind that nothing produces
decays exponentially and disappears.

### A worked example

The default network (`seed=1`, 10 kinds, printed below the formal
specification) has 42 reactions. Here are the three that the pair `X4 + X6`
catalyses, with their rate constants rounded:

```
X4 + X6 -> X4 + X6 + X1      α = 0.082
X4 + X6 -> X4 + X6 + X9      α = 0.826
X4 + X6 -> X4 + X6 + X10     α = 0.093
```

The second is the only reaction in the network that makes `X9`. So `X9`
survives only as long as both `X4` and `X6` do, and its concentration is
settled by a balance: production `0.826 · x4 · x6` against washout
`x9 · φ`. Integrating the network from a random mixture (the helper is in
*Using it* below) gives, at the fixed point, `x4 = 0.1247`, `x6 = 0.0456`
and `φ = 0.2091`. The balance then predicts `x9 = 0.826 × 0.1247 × 0.0456 /
0.2091 = 0.0225`, which is the value the integration reaches.
`X9` ends up the rarest kind: it has a single production route, and that
route needs `X6`, the second rarest. The other kinds each have
between three and eight production routes. In this network every kind is
produced by some pair of kinds that also survive, so all ten persist.

### When only some survive

The picture changes when the table is sparse. With `density=0.02` and
`seed=4` the network has only eight reactions. Two of them are

```
2X6 -> 2X6 + X7              α = 0.954
2X7 -> 2X7 + X6              α = 0.627
```

Pairs of `X6` make `X7`, and pairs of `X7` make `X6`. Neither kind copies
itself, but together they sustain each other. Everything else dies out, and
the tank ends with `X6` at 0.465 and `X7` at 0.535. This small cycle is what
the book describes when it says that "only a subset of species has survived
due to their mutually catalytic interactions". No reaction among `X6` and `X7` makes
anything outside the pair, and each member is made from within the pair: in
the language of chemical organisation theory (book Part IV) the set is
*closed* and *self-maintaining*, an *organisation*.

### The quantities in the specification

The formal specification below writes the rate constant of the reaction that
turns the ordered pair `(i, j)` into `k` as `α^k_ij`, and the total reactivity
of a pair, whatever it makes, as `a_ij = Σ_k α^k_ij`. The dilution flux is
then `φ = Σ_ij a_ij x_i x_j`, the total production. Because `Xi + Xj` and
`Xj + Xi` are the same collision, Chemart draws one reaction per unordered
pair, whose rate stands for the two ordered terms of the equation together.
Stadler and colleagues show that the equation only depends on these symmetric
sums, so nothing is lost. The reactor is an ODE integrator; in Chemart's
record the dilution appears as `outflow = "constant-total"`.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). n abstract species X_1..X_n with no internal structure

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 2). X_i + X_j --alpha^k_ij--&gt; X_i + X_j + X_k (both reactants catalytic)

x_k' = sum_ij alpha^k_ij x_i x_j - x_k phi(t), with phi = sum_ij a_ij x_i x_j and a_ij = sum_k alpha^k_ij

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time).

*How the population is bounded:* non-specific dilution flux phi

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("random-catalytic-networks", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
random-catalytic-networks: 10 species, 42 reactions, status=complete
provides: catalysts, flow, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
X1 + X2 -> X1 + X2 + X3  [mass-action k=0.7535131086748066]
X1 + X5 -> X1 + X5 + X4  [mass-action k=0.5285892632600216]
X1 + X5 -> X1 + X5 + X7  [mass-action k=0.641328169139375]
X1 + X7 -> X1 + X7 + X5  [mass-action k=0.8552269742870702]
X1 + X8 -> X1 + X8 + X2  [mass-action k=0.6457208955749478]
X1 + X9 -> X1 + X9 + X7  [mass-action k=0.6734598871529389]
X1 + X10 -> X1 + X10 + X8  [mass-action k=0.8254878133935558]
2 X2 -> 2 X2 + X7  [mass-action k=0.2624947127501015]
… and 34 more
```

The default call builds 10 kinds and keeps each possible reaction with
probability `density = 0.1`, drawing its rate uniformly between 0 and 1.
There are `55 × 8 = 440` possible reactions (55 unordered pairs, 8 products
each once self-copies are excluded), so about 44 exist; the default network
has 42. The species are just the names `X1` to `Xn`, `net.extras` is empty,
and there is no initial state: the published experiments start from a random
mixture, and you choose it.

Chemart generates the network but does not integrate it. This helper does,
from a random mixture drawn with `seed`, and returns the final concentrations
and the dilution flux `φ`:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import chemart

def steady_state(net, t_end=2000.0, seed=0):
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    S, R = (P - R).toarray(), R.toarray()
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    def f(t, x):
        v = k * np.prod(np.maximum(x, 0.0)[:, None] ** R, axis=0)  # mass action
        dx = S @ v                                                   # production
        return dx - x * dx.sum() / x.sum()                           # dilution phi
    x0 = np.random.default_rng(seed).dirichlet(np.ones(len(ids)))
    x = solve_ivp(f, (0, t_end), x0, method="LSODA", rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12).y[:, -1]
    phi = (S @ (k * np.prod(x[:, None] ** R, axis=0))).sum()
    return dict(zip(ids, x)), phi
```

**The default network settles to one interior fixed point.** Three different
random starting mixtures reach the same concentrations, with every kind
present:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("random-catalytic-networks", seed=1)
for start in range(3):
    x, phi = steady_state(net, t_end=4000, seed=start)
    print([round(float(v), 4) for v in x.values()], round(phi, 4))
```

```
[0.0964, 0.1297, 0.1089, 0.1247, 0.1003, 0.0456, 0.1452, 0.1092, 0.0225, 0.1175] 0.2091
[0.0964, 0.1297, 0.1089, 0.1247, 0.1003, 0.0456, 0.1452, 0.1092, 0.0225, 0.1175] 0.2091
[0.0964, 0.1297, 0.1089, 0.1247, 0.1003, 0.0456, 0.1452, 0.1092, 0.0225, 0.1175] 0.2091
```

**Sparser tables leave a surviving subset.** Lower `density` and count the
kinds above `1e-6` after integrating to `t = 20000`. Some sparse networks have
no self-sustaining set at all: production and `φ` then decay slowly towards
zero and the tank never settles. Count only the runs whose `φ` stays above
`1e-3`, which the table calls *active* after the paper's term for a system
whose flux stays positive. Over seeds 0 to 19 with `n = 10`:

```
density   runs that stay active   mean survivors
0.2       20 of 20                10.0
0.1       20 of 20                10.0
0.07      20 of 20                 8.9
0.05      13 of 20                 8.5
0.03       3 of 20                 5.7
```

The two-kind cycle of `X6` and `X7` shown above is `density=0.02, seed=4`.

**Direct replication sharpens competition.** With
`allow_direct_replication=True`, reactions such as `Xi + Xj -> Xi + Xj + Xi`
are allowed too. At `density=0.05`, over the same 20 seeds, 14 runs stay
active and they keep 6.0 kinds on average instead of 8.5; in three of them a
single kind takes over the tank. At `density=0.1` the effect is small (9.85
survivors instead of 10). `alpha_distribution="exponential"` draws rates from
an exponential distribution with mean 1 instead; see the parameter table
below. All of these runs take a few seconds.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `n` | `int` | `10` | structural | number of species <br>`2` … `60` |
| `density` | `float` | `0.1` | structural | probability that a given reaction X_i + X_j -&gt; X_i + X_j + X_k exists; sparse to dense <br>`0` … `1` |
| `allow_direct_replication` | `bool` | `False` | structural | allow k = i or k = j; the book's interesting case forbids direct self-replication |
| `alpha_distribution` | `enum` | `uniform` | kinetic | distribution of the rate alpha of an existing reaction: uniform on [0, 1) or exponential with mean 1 <br>one of `uniform`, `exponential` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "2 decisions"

    - The book gives the reaction scheme, the ODE and the direct-replication switch, but not how alpha is drawn. Each existing reaction gets alpha from `alpha_distribution` (default uniform on [0, 1)).
    - Reactions are sampled per unordered reactant pair {i, j}. In the ODE the ordered terms alpha^k_ij and alpha^k_ji describe the same reaction, so one rate per pair loses nothing. The dilution phi is outflow = 'constant-total'.

## Results

**Random networks converge to a stable fixed point.** Stadler, Fontana and
Miller (1993) integrated several hundred random networks of 5 to 20 kinds with
no elastic (non-reacting) pairs and no self-copying. In almost all of them,
the system "converged to a globally stable fixed point in the interior of the
simplex", that is, a unique equilibrium in which every kind survives. In a few
cases it lost some kinds first, and what remained was always a single
self-maintaining set. Their paper's abstract calls this generic behaviour
"extremely robust". The book summarises it as convergence to a fixed point in
which only a mutually catalytic subset survives, and notes that such a fixed
point was later recognised as an organisation in the sense of chemical
organisation theory. As the runs above show, in Chemart both halves are true
at different densities: dense tables keep every kind, sparse ones keep a
subset. The paper also proves that any kind nothing produces disappears, and
that in a system whose flux stays positive a kind disappears once everything
that produces it has gone, so the survivors always contain production
pathways for all their members.

**How sparseness and self-copying shape the outcome.** The paper's Figure 1
scans 10-kind systems, 20 random networks per grid point, over two knobs: the
fraction of pairs that do not react (`p_el`) and the fraction of reacting
pairs that copy one of their members (`p_self`). The number of surviving kinds
stays at or near 10 until `p_el` reaches about 0.6, then drops quickly, a
transition the authors link to the strong connectivity of random directed
graphs, and which gets sharper in larger systems. Raising `p_self` has a
similar effect: self-copying kinds compete as in the replicator equation, and
fewer survive. The authors conclude that the main effect of individual
replicators is to introduce strong positive correlations among the
concentrations. The equilibrium flux `φ` falls roughly linearly as `p_el`
grows and rises with `p_self`.

**Special cases.** When every reaction copies one of its reactants, the
equation becomes the replicator equation, and through a coordinate change due
to Hofbauer the Lotka-Volterra equation. The paper also lists complementary
replication (as in RNA copying), the mutation-replication equation and Fontana's
Turing gas as special cases, and notes that its discrete-time analogue is the
general second-order model of population genetics.

**Engineered networks do more.** Complicated dynamics need structure that a
random table rarely has. Coupling five random 5-kind networks in a ring, each
helping to make the next, reproduces the relaxation oscillations of Eigen and
Schuster's hypercycle, with whole networks taking the place of single
replicators. A *life cycle*, in which pairs of kind `k` make kind `k + 1` and
pairs of the last kind make the first, has a single interior fixed point that
is stable for up to five kinds, borderline at six and unstable from seven on;
the paper shows the limit cycle around which a ten-kind life cycle
oscillates. (The preprint's theorem states stability for up to four kinds,
but its own inequality, and a check of the eigenvalues done for this page,
give five.) Adding one well-placed reaction collapses the ten-kind limit
cycle to a fixed point. The two-kind cycle of the sparse Chemart run above is
a life cycle of length two, with unequal rates.

**What Chemart reproduces.** The test
`test_random_catalytic_network_equation_and_no_direct_replication` (in
`tests/chemistries/test_w2_book.py`) checks that no reaction makes one of its
own reactants when direct replication is off, and that the rate equations of
a generated network, with Chemart's constant-total dilution, equal the
catalytic network equation 7.32 of the book at a random state. No test
integrates the network or checks the convergence results; the runs on this
page were made for it. The replicator and Lotka-Volterra special cases are
covered by the equation, but no parameter setting of this generator produces
them, because `allow_direct_replication` only adds self-copying reactions
alongside the others.

**How Chemart's ensemble differs from the paper's.** The book does not say
how the random table is drawn. The paper gives every reacting pair exactly one
product, chosen at random, and a rate uniform on (0, 1), or fixed at 1 in its
"0/1-model". Chemart instead keeps each possible reaction independently with
probability `density`, so a pair can make several kinds or none, and
`allow_direct_replication` does not reproduce the paper's `p_self`. The
qualitative results above match, but the paper's Figure 1 cannot be
reproduced number for number with this generator.
